A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same block-verification research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D support comparison, including the image-based Python listings in v2.

before.justification: v2 reports original PaLM-2 experiments measuring block efficiency and wall-clock speedup, including comparisons with token verification and greedy block verification.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds Vicuna/Spec-Bench results, batched comparisons with SpecTr and SpecInfer, and an empirical toy-model acceptance-length distribution.

M1.justification: The acceptance rules, residual distributions, speculative-decoding loop, and greedy variant in Algorithms 1–6 remain unchanged. Expanded explanations and the illustrative Python initialization edit do not establish a changed decoding method.

E1.justification: The eight original prompt datasets remain. Section 6.2 adds Spec-Bench evaluation covering multi-turn conversation, retrieval-augmented generation, summarization, translation, question answering, and mathematical reasoning, extending the evaluated task requirements beyond the earlier coverage.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates token verification and greedy block verification as comparators. v3 additionally evaluates SpecTr and SpecInfer in Appendix D.1/Table 5, extending comparisons to multiple-draft systems. These methods were discussed in v2 but were not experimentally compared there.

E3.justification: New protocols include Vicuna-7B-v1.3/Vicuna-68M evaluation with a 1024-token generation limit and temperatures 0.2, 0.6, and 1.0; a batch-size-8 comparison selecting two competitor drafts from {2,4,8}; and a toy simulation with draft length 10. The original PaLM-2 prompt counts and length limits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds temperature sensitivity analysis, an empirical acceptance-length comparison explaining block verification's behavior (Figure 3), and a batching study examining the tradeoff between block efficiency and actual latency. Existing draft-length, drafter-quality, and greedy-verification analyses are retained.

E5.justification: The retained tables preserve their three-run reporting and standard deviations where previously supplied. The new Vicuna table also averages three runs. No increased run count, new uncertainty estimator, confidence interval, or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: All retained empirical tables match numerically after renumbering. New Table 2 reports Vicuna block-efficiency improvements of 3.72–8.70% and wall-clock improvements of 1.66–6.07%. New Table 5 shows block verification achieving the highest batched wall-clock speedups despite lower block efficiency than SpecTr/SpecInfer. Figure 3 adds acceptance-tail results. Section 6.2's stated 6.7% maximum conflicts with Table 2's 6.07%.

T1.justification: Although the main theorem statements remain, Appendix B substantially revises their supporting mathematics: it adds Lemma 6 and its proof, changes conditional-probability calculations in the optimality argument, corrects the acceptance-probability index in Appendix B.3, and rewrites Lemma 4's case analysis. Definition 1 also explicitly specifies permitted inputs and outputs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of lossless joint verification, optimal expected token production, simple substitution for token verification, and reported 5–8% wall-clock gains. Renaming 'Strict improvement' to 'Optimal improvement' does not change the contribution's meaning.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly states that zero-temperature decoding receives no additional speedup and interprets larger gains at higher temperatures through coordinated acceptance randomness. It also explains the batching computation tradeoff and why wall-clock gains peak at intermediate draft lengths despite increasing block efficiency.

D1.justification: v3 newly discloses temperature 1.0 and batch size 1 for the retained PaLM-2 experiments, without establishing that those settings changed. It documents the new Vicuna checkpoints, single H100 GPU, generation limit, and competitor draft-count selection. Appendix A also changes the illustrative block-verification initialization from None to an empty list.

R1.justification: Section 7 newly acknowledges Hu and Huang's independent verification work and distinguishes its improvement guarantee from the claimed optimality here. Chiang et al. and Kwon et al. are added for Vicuna and serving context. The broader related-work organization remains; Xia et al.'s publication update is the same cited work.

P1.justification: The existing method and theory exposition is reorganized, with parameter intuition moved and expanded into separate distribution-matching and optimality explanations. Appendix B's proof exposition is substantially rewritten. Results and Appendix D gain clearer subdivisions, although the main section sequence and much introductory wording remain.

P2.justification: v3 adopts the ICLR layout throughout, places the residual-distribution box beside the algorithm comparison, adds the acceptance-distribution figure and two result tables, and replaces the appendix's code-image figures with typeset listings. Existing plots and result tables are retained with relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence previously confined to PaLM-2 and token/greedy comparisons: Vicuna experiments test transfer across model families and temperatures, while Appendix D.1 tests practical latency against external competitors under batching. Expanded and partly corrected proof arguments improve auditability. These gains outweigh localized defects, including the new token-verification argmin description conflicting with Algorithm 1 and the 6.7% versus 6.07% reporting discrepancy.
